issues.failure_explanation: The opening step of the Appendix B.1 derivation equates the random variable log q_theta(u_0|a), a function of u_0, with its expectation under p(u_0|a); this identity is false unless log q_theta(u_0|a) is p(.|a)-almost surely constant. Consequently the variational bounds of Sections 3.1 and 3.2, whose right-hand sides E_{p(u_{0:T})}[.] and E_{p(u_{0:T}|a)}[.] also average over u_0, do not hold pointwise in u_0 as written. Only the expected log-likelihood E_{p(u_0|a)}[-log q_theta(u_0|a)] obeys such a bound; a per-sample bound would require the expectation E_{p(u_{1:T}|u_0)} over the latents only.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the bound for the expected log-likelihood (wrap the left-hand sides in E_{p(u_0)}[.] or E_{p(u_0|a)}[.]), or re-derive the per-sample ELBO with E_{p(u_{1:T}|u_0)} and average afterwards; remove the false identity.
issues.overall_effect: The VLB inequalities of Sections 3.1-3.2 and the Appendix B.1 derivation are incorrect as stated. Once expectations are restored, the decomposition into L_T, L_{t-1}, L_0 and the training losses remain valid, so no labelled result is invalidated.
issues.title: Variational bound stated pointwise but valid only in expectation; derivation opens with a false identity
issues.why_classification: Routine local repair (restoring expectation signs, with two equivalent standard formulations); the decomposition, the losses, both propositions, and the algorithm are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Similarly, we can calculate $L_0$ and ignore the pre-factor which gives

issues.failure_explanation: In the noise-free case the prescribed reverse covariance at the final step is Sigma_theta(1) = ((1- ar\alpha_0)/(1- ar\alpha_1)) beta_1 I with  ar\alpha_0 = 1 (empty product), i.e. exactly 0. Then q_theta(u_0|u_1,a) is a Dirac measure, so the VLB term L_0 = E[-log q_theta(u_0|u_1,a)], a Gaussian negative log-likelihood with zero variance, is ill-defined (it diverges unless m_theta(1,u_1,a) = u_0 exactly). The claimed calculation of L_0 by ignoring the pre-factor is therefore invalid in the noise-free setting, since the implied weight 1/(2 Sigma_theta(1)) is infinite, and the derivation of the unified training loss from the VLB fails at t=1 for the paper's primary noise-free regime (the entropy-matching claim at t=1 is likewise degenerate). For Gaussian-noise data Sigma_theta(1) = beta_1 > 0 and the reduction is valid up to constants.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Treat the t=1 step separately, e.g. replace the degenerate L_0 with a non-degenerate decoder (a positive variance floor on the last reverse step), or restrict the VLB-to-epsilon-loss equivalence to t >= 2 and justify the t=1 term directly as mean matching.
issues.overall_effect: The VLB-based justification of the PDNO training objective is incomplete at the final diffusion step for noise-free data. The loss actually optimized (eqn:unified_L) and Algorithm alg:PDNO remain well defined and unaffected.
issues.title: Noise-free reverse covariance at t=1 is exactly zero, so the L_0 term of the VLB is ill-defined and its reduction to the epsilon loss is unsupported
issues.why_classification: A degenerate boundary case with a standard local fix; the method, the optimized loss, and all reported results survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the mean relative $L_2$-error (MRLE) and the mean standard deviation (MSTD) that are defined by
\# of samples $N_s$   &  $1$ if noise-free; $100$ if noisy

issues.failure_explanation: A sample standard deviation is already normalized by the sample count, so dividing its L_2 norm by N_s makes the defined quantity scale like 1/N_s; it is not a mean standard deviation (a relative variant would divide by ||u||_2, as the MRLE does), and no mathematical justification for the 1/N_s factor is given. In addition, the noise-free runs are specified with N_s = 1 (Tables A1-A4), for which the sample standard deviation is undefined or identically zero, so the nonzero noise-free MSTD values reported in Tables 1-3 cannot be produced by the stated procedure.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the definition (delete the spurious 1/N_s, or divide by ||u||_2 for a relative metric) and specify the sample count actually used to compute the reported MSTD values.
issues.overall_effect: The MSTD columns of Tables 1-3, the paper's reported uncertainty metrics, are not defined by the stated formula; the scale and provenance of the reported uncertainty numbers are unreliable.
issues.title: MSTD metric divides the sample standard deviation by the number of samples and is degenerate at the stated N_s = 1
issues.why_classification: Local correction of a metric definition with more than one plausible repair; no method, result, or guarantee depends on it, though the interpretation of the reported numbers changes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Suppose that the initial state $u_0$ follows a (nonzero mean) Gaussian distribution with the identity covariance, i.e., $u_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m, \mathbf{I})$
corrupting the output $u$ by an additive Gaussian noise $\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma(a))$, i.e., $u_{\eta} = u + \eta$
$\mathcal{D}_{\eta}$   & Noisy training data set whose outputs are corrupted by $\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathrm{I})$
The model is trained on the noisy data set with $\sigma=0.0005$

issues.failure_explanation: Proposition 2, and the subsequent claim that integrating out u_0 yields a reverse conditional with covariance beta_t I, hold only when u_0 given a has identity covariance. The paper's Gaussian-noise setting instead has u_0|a distributed as N(u(a), sigma^2 I) with sigma^2 != 1 (sigma = 1% or 5% in Test 1 with unnormalized data; sigma = 0.0005 and 0.001 in Test 2). For conditional variance s^2, integrating out u_0 gives Cov(u_{t-1}|u_t,a) = (( ar\alpha_{t-1} s^2 + 1 -  ar\alpha_{t-1}) beta_t)/( ar\alpha_t s^2 + 1 -  ar\alpha_t) I, which equals beta_t I only at s^2 = 1; for s^2 much smaller than 1 it approaches the noise-free value ((1- ar\alpha_{t-1})/(1- ar\alpha_t)) beta_t. The asserted entropy-matching optimality of Sigma_theta = beta_t I for Gaussian-noise data is therefore not established, and is false, in the regime the paper actually uses.

failure_location.quote: Hence, the parameterization~\eqref{eqn:cov} for $\Sigma_{\theta}$ in the Gaussian noise setting is optimal in the sense that $H_p(u_{t-1}|u_t) = H_{q_{\theta}}(u_{t-1}|u_t)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either restrict the optimality claim to data whose conditional distribution given a has unit covariance (e.g. after variance normalization), or derive and use the correct sigma-dependent reverse covariance (( ar\alpha_{t-1} sigma^2 + 1 -  ar\alpha_{t-1}) beta_t)/( ar\alpha_t sigma^2 + 1 -  ar\alpha_t) I.
issues.overall_effect: The theoretical justification of the noisy-data branch of the covariance prescription (eqn:cov), and of entropy matching in the noisy experiments, is unreliable for non-unit-variance noise. Proposition 2 itself remains valid and the prescription remains a usable heuristic.
issues.title: Optimality of the beta_t I reverse covariance for Gaussian-noise data asserted outside Proposition 2's identity-covariance hypothesis
issues.why_classification: The stated guarantee fails in the advertised noisy-data regime; repairing it requires either a limited weakening of the claim's scope or a contained new covariance derivation, while the method, the experiments, and Proposition 2 survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \mathbb{E}_{q_{\theta}}\left[-\log q_{\theta}(u_{0:T}) \right] = H_{q_{\theta}}(u_T) + \sum_{t=1}^T H_{q_{\theta}}(u_{t-1} | u_t) = H_p(u_T) + \sum_{t=1}^T H_p(u_{t-1} | u_t) = \mathbb{E}_{p}\left[-\log p(u_{0:T}) \right]
where $\beta_t$ is the variance schedule such that the final state $u_T$ is approximately standard normal for $T$ sufficiently large
Since $q_{\theta}(u_T)$ is assumed to be a standard Gaussian, $L_T$ is independent of the parameter $\theta$.

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed chain only compares trajectory entropies under each model's own law, and even that fails. First, equality of (conditional) entropies does not establish exact likelihood: the relevant cross-entropy E_p[-log q_theta(u_{0:T})] equals E_p[-log p(u_{0:T})] only if q_theta = p, which is not shown. Second, the middle equality H_{q_theta}(u_T) = H_p(u_T) fails in the noise-free case, where conditioned on a (the setting of Proposition 1) p(u_T|a) = N(sqrt( ar\alpha_T) u(a), (1- ar\alpha_T) I) has entropy (n/2) log(2 pi e (1- ar\alpha_T)), different from (n/2) log(2 pi e) = H_{q_theta}(u_T). Third, in the Gaussian case the entropies match but q_theta(u_T) = N(0, I) differs from p(u_T|a) = N(sqrt( ar\alpha_T) m, I), so the induced q_theta(u_0|a) differs from p(u_0|a) in mean; the paper itself concedes the terminal law is only approximately standard normal. Hence the model does not achieve the exact likelihood in either case.

failure_location.quote: In both cases, the noise-free and Gaussian noise, the learned parametric model $q_{\theta}$ achieves the exact likelihood under the true model $p$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the claim with the correct weaker statement: with a perfect noise predictor the reverse conditionals match the true ones per step, and the data-level law, hence the likelihood, is matched only up to the terminal mismatch between p(u_T|.) and the standard-Gaussian prior.
issues.overall_effect: The concluding theoretical claim of the covariance-choice appendix is false; the covariance prescriptions of eqn:cov are left with only per-step, assumption-laden justifications.
issues.title: Closing claim that the model achieves the exact likelihood does not follow: entropy matching is not likelihood matching and the terminal laws differ
issues.why_classification: The exactness claim must be withdrawn and replaced by an approximate statement (a limited weakening with a contained reformulation); no other result depends on it and the method is unaffected.
